claim: Theory of mind is thought to provide a causal and flexible cognitive framework that allows humans to navigate complex social interactions.
source: Theory of mind is thought to provide a causal and flexible cognitive framework that allows humans to navigate complex social interactions (FeldmanHall and Shenhav, 2019; Tamir and Thornton, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to FeldmanHall and Shenhav, 2019 and Tamir and Thornton, 2018.

claim: Through theory of mind, different observable social cues can be used to infer otherwise imperceptible mental states such that the behaviour of other individuals can be interpreted, predicted, and manipulated based on an interplay of different mental states.
source: Through this framework, different observable social cues can be used to infer otherwise imperceptible mental states (e.g., perspectives, desires, knowledge, beliefs), such that the behaviour of other individuals can be interpreted, predicted, and manipulated based on an interplay of different mental states (Baker et al., 2017; Bartsch and Wellman, 1989; Bennett and Galpert, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Baker et al., 2017; Bartsch and Wellman, 1989; Bennett and Galpert, 1992.

claim: In humans, theory of mind is thought to emerge as a stepwise process, with a meta-representational framework in place by at least 5 years of age.
source: In humans, theory of mind is thought to emerge as a stepwise process, with a meta-representational framework in place by at least 5 years of age (Wellman, 2018; Wellman and Liu, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wellman, 2018 and Wellman and Liu, 2004.

claim: Before developing meta-representational theory of mind, infants can already respond to multiple pieces of social information in an integrated manner.
source: However, even before they develop this meta-representational theory of mind, infants can already respond to multiple pieces of social information in an integrated manner (e.g., Moses et al., 2001; Repacholi et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moses et al., 2001 and Repacholi et al., 2014.

claim: Infants seem to implicitly register social cues and exhibit adaptive responses accordingly.
source: At a minimum, though, infants seem to implicitly register social cues and exhibit adaptive responses accordingly (Apperly and Butterfill, 2009; Butterfill and Apperly, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Apperly and Butterfill, 2009 and Butterfill and Apperly, 2013.

claim: Corvids are a group of large-brained birds that are hypothesised to have evolved sophisticated cognitive abilities independently from primates.
source: Corvids are a group of large-brained birds that are hypothesised to have evolved sophisticated cognitive abilities independently from primates (Clayton and Emery, 2015; Emery and Clayton, 2004; Güntürkün and Bugnyar, 2016; Osvath et al., 2014; Seed et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clayton and Emery, 2015; Emery and Clayton, 2004; Güntürkün and Bugnyar, 2016; Osvath et al., 2014; Seed et al., 2009.

claim: Previous research has reported that Eurasian jays may be able to adjust their behaviour according to cues that correlate with the perspective and current desire of a conspecific.
source: In particular, previous research has reported that Eurasian jays (Garrulus glandarius) may be able to adjust their behaviour according to cues that correlate with the perspective and current desire of a conspecific.
evidence: The claim is based on a summary of previous research findings mentioned in the manuscript.

claim: Eurasian jays have been reported to preferentially cache food in less visible locations in the presence of a conspecific competitor.
source: In the presence of a conspecific competitor, these jays have been reported to preferentially cache food in less visible locations (e.g., behind barriers, at distance), or in non-noisy substrates, which has been interpreted as a potential response to the visual (Legg et al., 2016; Legg and Clayton, 2014) or acoustic perspective (Shaw and Clayton, 2013) of a potential pilferer.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Legg et al., 2016; Legg and Clayton, 2014; and Shaw and Clayton, 2013.

claim: Male Eurasian jays change the type of food shared with their female partner, depending on which food the female has been sated on.
source: In parallel, research investigating food-sharing behaviour found that male Eurasian jays change the type of food shared with their female partner, depending on which food the female has been sated on, and therefore which she desires (Ostojić et al., 2013; Ostojić et al., 2014; Ostojić et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ostojić et al., 2013; Ostojić et al., 2014; Ostojić et al., 2016.

claim: Eurasian jays and Western scrub-jays preferentially cached food that an observer was sated on.
source: In a recent study, a similar response to another's satiety has also been reported in the context of caching, whereby Eurasian jays and Western scrub-jays preferentially cached food that an observer, and thus potential pilferer, was sated on Ostojić et al., 2017.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ostojić et al., 2017.

claim: The effect reported by Ostojić et al., 2017 was unlikely to be based on theory of mind because the caching jays showed this effect also when they did not know what food the observer was pre-fed on.
source: Notably, the effect reported in this study was unlikely to be based on theory of mind because the caching jays showed this effect also when they did not know what food the observer was pre-fed on and when the only cue available was the observer's behaviour during the caching event itself (Ostojić et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on interpretation of findings from Ostojić et al., 2017.

claim: In Experiment 1, jays did not cache a higher proportion of food items in the out-of-view tray in the Different Food condition compared to the Same Food condition.
source: In contrast to the first prediction, a comparison of the proportion of items cached in the out-of-view tray between the Different Food and the Same Food conditions did not detect a statistically significant difference (Wilcoxon signed-rank test: n = 7, W = 13, P = 0.21; Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and reference to Figure 1.

claim: In Experiment 1, the proportion of items cached in the out-of-view tray was not significantly different from chance in the Different Food condition.
source: In contrast to the second prediction, the proportion of items cached in the out-of-view tray was not significantly different from that expected by chance in the Different Food condition (one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test: n = 7, W = 25, p=0.11).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: In Experiment 1, the numerical pattern of the jays' caching was in the opposite direction to the prediction: jays' caching was more biased towards the out-of-view tray in the Same Food than the Different Food condition.
source: Notably, the numerical pattern of the jays' caching was in the opposite direction to the prediction: jays' caching was more biased towards the out-of-view tray in the Same Food than the Different Food condition (Proportion of items cached out-of-view: MedianSame Food = 0.5, MedianDifferent Food = 0.17; Caches out-of-view minus Caches in-view: MedianSame Food = 0, MedianDifferent Food = –2).
evidence: The claim is supported by descriptive statistics from the experiment.

claim: In Experiment 2, no statistically significant difference in the proportion of P cached was detected between the In-view and the Out-of-view conditions.
source: A comparison of the proportion of P cached between the In-view and the Out-of-view conditions – [Pcached/(Pcached+ Mcached)]pre-fed P – [Pcached/(Pcached+ Mcached)]pre-fed M – did not detect a statistically significant difference (MedianIn-view = 0, MedianOut-of-view = 0; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: n = 7, W = 3, p=0.83; Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and reference to Figure 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, in the In-view condition, no statistically significant difference in the proportion of P cached could be detected between the trials in which observer was sated on peanuts and the trials in which the observer was sated on macadamia nuts.
source: In the In-view condition, no statistically significant difference in the proportion of P cached could be detected between the trials in which observer was sated on peanuts and the trials in which the observer was sated on macadamia nuts (Medianpre-fed P = 0.33, Medianpre-fed M = 0.5; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: n = 7, W = 3, p=0.83).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: In Experiment 3, the proportion of the items cached in the out-of-view tray was not significantly higher in the Observed condition than in the Private condition.
source: The proportion of the items cached in the out-of-view tray was not significantly higher in the Observed condition than in the Private condition (MedianObserved = 0.71, MedianPrivate = 0.54; Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 7, W = 2, pone-tailed = 0.59).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: In Experiment 4, the average proportion of items cached in the out-of-view tray was not significantly higher in the Observed condition than in the Private condition.
source: In the same analysis that was used by Legg and Clayton, 2014, the average proportion of items cached in the out-of-view tray was not significantly higher in the Observed condition than in the Private condition (MedianObserved = 0.5, MedianPrivate = 0.44; Permutation test, n = 7, Z = 0.15, pone-tailed=0.56).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results using the same method as the original study.

claim: Experiments 3 and 4 consistently did not detect the effect originally reported by Legg and Clayton, 2014.
source: Taken together, Experiments 3 and 4 consistently did not detect the effect originally reported by Legg and Clayton, 2014, whereby Eurasian jays adjusted their caching pattern to the transparency and opaqueness of the barrier around the caching tray specifically when an observer was present during the caching event (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results from Experiments 3 and 4, and reference to Figure 3.

claim: In Experiment 5, no statistically significant difference could be detected in the proportion of P cached between the Barrier and No-barrier conditions.
source: No statistically significant difference could be detected in difference of the proportion of P cached when the observer was sated on P minus the proportion of P cached when observer was sated on M – [Pcached /(Pcached+ Mcached)pre-fed P] – [Pcached /(Pcached+ Mcached)pre-fed M] – between the Barrier and No-barrier conditions (MedianBarrier = 0, MedianNo Barrier = −0.04; Wilcoxon signed-rank test: n = 7, W = 11, p=0.18).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: In Experiment 5, in both conditions, no statistically significant difference could be detected in the proportion of P cached between the two pre-feeding trials.
source: In addition, in both conditions, no statistically significant difference could be detected in the proportion of P cached between the two pre-feeding trials (Barrier condition: Medianpre-fed P = 0.17, Medianpre-fed M = 0.1, Wilcoxon signedrank test, n = 7, W=-2, pone-tailed=0.43; No-barrier condition: Medianpre-fed P = 0,12, Medianpre-fed M = 0,25, n = 7, W=-9, pone-tailed=0.91).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results.

claim: The results from Experiment 5 cannot be interpreted as providing support for the idea that the presence of the barrier may be the reason why the results in Experiment 2 did not detect the same pattern as the one reported in Ostojić et al., 2017.
source: Thus, the results from Experiment 5 cannot be interpreted as providing support for the idea that the presence of the barrier may be the reason why the results in Experiment 2 did not detect the same pattern as the one reported in Ostojić et al., 2017.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental results.

claim: Across five experiments, there was little evidence that Eurasian jays adjusted their caching behaviour in line with the visual perspective and current desire of another agent.
source: Across five experiments, which also include replications of previous work, we found little evidence that our jays adjusted their caching behaviour in line with the visual perspective and current desire of another agent, neither by integrating these social cues nor by responding to only one type of cue independently.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined results from all five experiments reported in the manuscript.

claim: In four of the seven tests of the hypothesis that the jays could use social cues to protect their caches, the results were not in the direction of the prediction.
source: Specifically, in four of the seven tests of the hypothesis that the jays could use social cues to protect their caches, the results were not in the direction of the prediction: Experiment 1, prediction 1; Experiment 2, predictions 1 and 2; Experiment 5, prediction 2, No-barrier condition.
evidence: The claim is supported by summary of results across multiple experiments.

claim: Each of the experiments likely had low power to detect theoretically meaningful effect sizes.
source: First, each of our experiments likely had low power to detect theoretically meaningful, and perhaps the most theoretically plausible, effect sizes.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the statistical properties of the experimental design.

claim: The failure to find any significant results across five experiments suggests that the original effect sizes might be overestimated.
source: However, that we failed to find any significant results across five experiments with similar designs to the original studies shows that no extremely large effect sizes were present in our jays and suggests that the original effect sizes might be overestimated – which would be expected if the original studies came from a series of underpowered research combined with a publication bias (Farrar et al., 2020; Fiedler and Prager, 2018; Hedges, 1984).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the pattern of results and supported by citations about publication bias and statistical power.

claim: The birds tested in the current study were around 5 years older than when they were tested in the previous studies.
source: Second, our five studies used the same populations of birds as tested in the previous studies (Legg and Clayton, 2014; Ostojić et al., 2017; Table 1), but they were around 5 years older.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 and comparison with previous studies.

claim: It is possible that the behaviour of the birds has changed over time, for example as a result of aging and/or learning effects.
source: It is possible that the behaviour of these birds has changed over time, for example as a result of aging and/or learning effects.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about potential explanations for the results.

claim: The overall number of cached items does not appear too dissimilar in the current experiments and the previous studies.
source: The overall number of cached items (as a proxy for cache motivation) does not appear too dissimilar in the current experiments and the previous studies (see Figure 5 for a comparison of the number of items cached per bird per trial across all of the experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 5 showing comparative data.

claim: Research in primates has shown that motivations potentially relevant to cache protection, such as those driving socialisation and social influence, change dramatically throughout life, declining substantially in some taxa.
source: Although data on corvids specifically are limited, research in primates has shown that motivations potentially relevant to cache protection, such as those driving socialisation and social influence, change dramatically throughout life, declining substantially in some taxa (Machanda and Rosati, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Machanda and Rosati, 2020.

claim: Rhesus macaques show a reduced propensity to follow gaze in older age.
source: A notable example of this process is provided by rhesus macaques, which, similarly to humans, show a reduced propensity to follow gaze in older age (Rosati et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rosati et al., 2016.

claim: Previous studies with Western scrub-jays suggested that the caching behaviour itself is underpinned by a motivational system that acts as a compulsion to cache and that is not sensitive to reinforcement or other external conditions.
source: With regard to potential changes due to prior experience and learning, previous studies with Western scrub-jays suggested that the caching behaviour itself is underpinned by a motivational system that acts as a compulsion to cache and that is not sensitive to reinforcement or other external conditions and that a second motivational system influences decision making during caching through sensitivity to conditions at cache retrieval (Clayton et al., 2005; de Kort et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Clayton et al., 2005 and de Kort et al., 2007.

claim: In the laboratory, caching experiments are conducted such that an observer is located in an adjacent compartment and cannot access the conspecific's caches.
source: In our laboratory, caching experiments are conducted such that an observer is located in an adjacent compartment and cannot access the conspecific's caches, and in retrieval sessions the jays also receive feedback that their caches are unaffected by conditions at caching.
evidence: The claim describes the experimental procedures used in the laboratory.

claim: The Eurasian jays regularly cache outside of testing time.
source: This issue is likely exacerbated by the fact that our Eurasian jays regularly cache outside of testing time, such that laboratory conditions do not impair the natural intensity of caching behaviour exhibited by this species (Goodwin, 1951; Goodwin, 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by observation and citations to Goodwin, 1951 and Goodwin, 1986.

claim: Eurasian jays are not currently housed in any other laboratory in the world.
source: Unfortunately, it is unlikely that a study like the one above could be conducted in a near future on the same species of corvids because Eurasian jays are not currently housed in any other laboratory in the world, and there is no guarantee that a new colony will be acquired by our laboratory.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the availability of Eurasian jays in research facilities.

claim: The results conflict with a larger body of literature on cache-protection strategies in corvids.
source: Our results conflict not just with the two studies that our research was built on Legg and Clayton, 2014; Ostojić et al., 2017, but also, more generally, with a larger body of literature on cache-protection strategies in corvids (Bugnyar et al., 2016; Dally et al., 2004; Dally et al., 2005; Emery and Clayton, 2001; Heinrich and Pepper, 1998) and Eurasian jays in particular (Legg et al., 2016; Shaw and Clayton, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with multiple cited studies.

claim: In the cooperative context of food sharing, the effect whereby males adjust the pattern of food shared with the female to her specific satiety has been reliably shown by the same males in subsequent studies.
source: For example, in the cooperative context of food sharing, the effect whereby males adjust the pattern of food shared with the female to her specific satiety (Ostojić et al., 2013) has been reliably shown by the same males in subsequent studies (Legg, 2015; Ostojić et al., 2014; Ostojić et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies showing consistent results.

claim: Food sharing is an integral part of jays' courtship behaviour and is important not only in establishing but also maintaining the pair bond.
source: Food sharing is an integral part of jays' courtship behaviour and is important not only in establishing but also maintaining the pair bond (Goodwin, 1951).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Goodwin, 1951.

claim: Concerning the failed replication of Ostojić et al., 2017, a further, unpublished, replication attempt also did not detect the originally reported effects.
source: Concerning our failed replication of Ostojić et al., 2017, a slightly different reasoning applies as, to our knowledge, no similar study has been conducted in another laboratory. As such, we believe we have access to all the data on this topic. These are the current study, the Ostojić et al., 2017 study, and a further, unpublished, replication attempt that also did not detect the originally reported effects (Crosby, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to an unpublished replication attempt by Crosby, 2019.

claim: Understanding the extent of publication bias in the comparative cognition literature is key to understanding their evidential value.
source: First, understanding the extent of publication bias in our literature is key to understanding their evidential value.
evidence: The claim is based on reasoning about research methodology and validity.

claim: Replication and extension studies, conducted in a two-step process, present a useful procedure for comparative cognition research.
source: For example, replication and extension studies, conducted in a two-step process, such as have been traditionally employed in comparative cognition (Beran, 2018), present a useful procedure.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Beran, 2018 and reasoning about research methodology.

claim: Fourteen adult Eurasian jays from two separate colonies were tested in this study.
source: Fourteen adult Eurasian jays from two separate colonies were tested in this study (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 1 showing participant information.

claim: All of the jays were hand-raised, having been taken as chicks from wild nests or from the natural nests of birds in a breeding programme.
source: All of the jays were hand-raised, having been taken as chicks from wild nests or from the natural nests of birds in a breeding programme.
evidence: The claim describes the origin and rearing of the study subjects.

claim: All procedures were approved by the University of Cambridge Animal Ethics Committee (reference n. ZOO35/17).
source: All procedures were approved by the University of Cambridge Animal Ethics Committee (reference n. ZOO35/17).
evidence: The claim is a statement about ethical approval for the research.

claim: In Experiment 1, seven birds met the criterion in the familiarisation and proceeded to the test.
source: All birds except two reached the criterion in the familiarisation, that is they cached at least one item on each trial, and therefore proceeded to the test (leading to n = 7 for the test).
evidence: The claim is supported by data about participant inclusion in the experiment.

claim: In Experiment 2, seven birds passed the familiarisation and proceeded to the test.
source: All birds except one (Lisbon; Table 1) passed the familiarisation and proceeded to the test.
evidence: The claim is supported by data about participant inclusion in the experiment.

claim: In Experiment 3, seven birds' data were included in the analysis.
source: The analysis included the data of seven birds, that is, all birds except one (Lisbon).
evidence: The claim is supported by data about participant inclusion in the analysis.

claim: In Experiment 4, nine birds passed the familiarisation and proceeded to the test.
source: Nine birds passed the familiarisation and proceeded to the test.
evidence: The claim is supported by data about participant inclusion in the experiment.

claim: In Experiment 5, all eight birds passed the familiarisation and proceeded to the test.
source: All eight birds (Table 1) passed the familiarisation and proceeded to the test.
evidence: The claim is supported by data about participant inclusion in the experiment.

claim: Experiment 4 was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework.
source: This experiment was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/8p4tx/).
evidence: The claim is a statement about the pre-registration of the experiment.

claim: Experiment 5 was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework.
source: This experiment was pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/8p4tx/).
evidence: The claim is a statement about the pre-registration of the experiment.

claim: No power analysis was conducted to establish an appropriate sample size for the study.
source: No power analysis was conducted to establish an appropriate sample size for the study.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the study design methodology.

claim: The T-barrier consisted of three plastic panels forming two arms and one stem, with one arm constructed out of transparent Perspex and the other arm and stem constructed out of white opaque Perspex.
source: This barrier consisted of three plastic panels (25 × 40 cm) forming two arms and one stem. One arm of the 'T' was constructed out of transparent Perspex, while the other arm and the stem were constructed out of white opaque Perspex.
evidence: The claim describes the physical properties of the experimental apparatus.

claim: The U-barrier consisted of two lateral Perspex panels and one central Perspex panel forming two angles of approximately 45°.
source: The barrier consisted of two lateral Perspex panels (26 × 25 cm) and one central Perspex panel (53 × 25 cm) forming two angles of approximately 45°.
evidence: The claim describes the physical properties of the experimental apparatus.

claim: Legg and Clayton, 2014 found that jays cached a higher proportion of food items in the out-of-view tray in the Observed than in the Private conditions.
source: The authors compared the jays' caching pattern in the Private condition with that in the Observed conditions (the two observed conditions were merged together), and found that jays cached a higher proportion of food items in the out-of-view tray in the Observed than in the Private conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to and description of findings from Legg and Clayton, 2014.

claim: Ostojić et al., 2017 found that the jays' preference for caching food A over food B was larger after the observer was sated on food A than after the observer was sated on food B.
source: Ostojić et al., 2017 found that the jays' preference for caching food A over food B was larger after the observer was sated on food A than after the observer was sated on food B.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to and description of findings from Ostojić et al., 2017.

claim: When data were re-analysed for Eurasian jays only, the effect reported by Ostojić et al., 2017 was still statistically significant in the Seen condition but not in the Unseen condition.
source: Note that, when data were re-analysed for Eurasian jays only, the effect was still statistically significant in the Seen condition – although it was not statistically significant in the Unseen condition (Crosby, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a re-analysis by Crosby, 2019.
